mbahist: Mount Bachelor Academy, "MBA History" (school website, archived 2002)
columbian: Associated Press via The Columbian, 1998 (archived listing)
naas: Northwest Association of Accredited Schools, list of accredited Oregon schools
ccso: Crook County Sheriff's Office, case no. 982737 (December 1998)
nautilus: Nautilus Insurance Corp. v. Mount Bachelor Educational Center, Inc., No. 3:12-cv-00825-SI (D. Or. Dec. 21, 2012), opinion and order

paragraphs: Mount Bachelor Academy was a therapeutic boarding school for teenagers about 26 miles east of Prineville, Oregon, owned by Aspen Education Group.{bulletin09} It took its first students in 1988 and by 2009 charged $6,400 a month.{mbahist,ore09} Complaints that it mistreated students reached the press as early as 1998.{columbian} In November 2009, after a seven-month investigation, Oregon found that students had been sexually humiliated and abused in its "Lifesteps" seminars and suspended its license, and the school closed for good that December.{kohd,bulletin09,ore09} From July 2011 to January 2012 former students brought three lawsuits over abuse going back to the 1990s, which ended in confidential settlements in 2014.{ce_nine,nautilus,bul15}

By the school's own account, Barry Weiss of College Health Enterprises, a group of Southern California hospitals, approached the educator Linda Houghton in 1987 about starting an emotional-growth boarding school.{mbahist,bul09b} After permit trouble in Powell Butte, the school was built at the former Mark's Creek Lodge in the Ochoco National Forest.{mbahist} It took its first students in 1988, with Houghton as executive director, and graduated its first class in December 1990.{mbahist} Its methods came from CEDU, the California school whose founder, Mel Wasserman, drew on the Synanon movement, and Lifesteps workshops were part of its program from the start.{bul09b,mbahist} Tim Brace was executive director from 1993 to 1997.{mbahist,bulletin09} Sharon Bitz, who had worked at the school for eight years, took over in May 1997 and ran it until it closed.{mbahist,bulletin09} In 1998 College Health Enterprises spun the school and other youth programs off into Aspen Youth Services, later renamed Aspen Education Group.{mbahist,bul09b} In 2006 CRC Health Group, owned by the private equity firm Bain Capital, bought Aspen.{bul09b,buyouts} Oregon's Department of Human Services licensed the school.{w0307} Its academic program was accredited by the Northwest Association of Accredited Schools.{naas}

In 1998 the Associated Press reported that former employees and parents said teens were mistreated at the academy.{columbian} That March four former employees and two parents alleged that students were deprived of sleep, subjected to obscenity-laced tirades and made to work overnight in near-freezing temperatures.{columbian} The Oregon Department of Human Services investigated and cleared the program.{time09} In December 1998 a 17-year-old student, Brandon H., died outside the facility; the Crook County sheriff and coroner investigated and ruled his death a suicide.{ccso} By 2009 the school was licensed for 125 students and had 88, with 77 staff.{time09,ore09} Students were 14 to 17½ years old and typically stayed 14 to 16 months.{time09,ore09}

The state's investigation began after complaints in the spring of 2009.{kohd,bul09b} From 2009 on, former students described the Lifesteps seminars to reporters.{time09,mj,time11} An 18-year-old whom TIME called Jane told the writer Maia Szalavitz that April, "They had me dress up as a French maid," and "I had to sit on guys' laps and give them lap dances."{time09} Bitz called the reports "inaccurate representations" and said some accusations were "demonstrably false".{time09} On November 3, 2009, the Department of Human Services confirmed nine allegations of abuse and neglect involving five students since 2007, most of them in Lifesteps.{kohd,world,bulletin09} Investigators found sexualized role-play in front of other students, students made to re-enact past physical and sexual abuse, sleep deprivation, manual labor and forced exercise as punishment, and bans on speaking and on phone calls home.{bul09b,kohd,world} They called the Lifesteps workshops "punitive, humiliating, degrading and traumatizing".{bul09b} The school had one Oregon-licensed mental health professional and no staff qualified to treat substance abuse or eating disorders.{bulletin09} The state suspended its license, gave it 90 days to correct the violations and filed a complaint against Bitz, saying she knew or should have known of the abuse.{bulletin09,ore09}

Aspen did not try to reopen.{ore09} On November 9, 2009, it announced the school would close permanently by December 9, eliminating 69 to 72 jobs.{ore09} It blamed "the revocation of the Facility's operating license," though the state said it had only suspended the license.{ore09} The school and Bitz fought the findings in four legal proceedings from December 2009 to July 2010.{co10} They settled in October 2010.{co10} The department replaced "substantiated" in its findings with a statement that it had "reasonable cause to believe that abuse or neglect occurred," and the school acknowledged the department had a reasonable basis to investigate.{co10} The findings against Bitz would be withdrawn only if she completed a two-year course in child and adolescent psychology.{co10} A department spokesman, Gene Evans, said, "The settlement does not exonerate MBA."{time11}

On July 6, 2011, nine former students sued the school, Aspen and CRC Health in Multnomah County for $14.25 million, alleging emotional, physical and sexual abuse in the 1990s.{ce_nine,orlive_nine,chn,time11} Their complaint listed "exposure to the elements; extreme cold; extreme heat; forced standing; forcible and unnecessary physical restraint; denial of meals; sleep deprivation" and "extreme forms of punitive labor for no pay."{chn} It said Lifesteps sessions required "making known victims of child sexual abuse act out sexual propositioning and activities on or with other residents as well as adult staff."{chn} The state had recovered bedsheets bearing sexual slurs such as "whore" and "slut".{time11} The school denied the claims and said it had provided a nurturing environment.{orlive_stmt} By late August 2011 the suit, MLM v. Mount Bachelor Educational Center (No. 1107-08552), had 17 plaintiffs seeking $25.5 million, and that November a judge ruled it would be tried in Prineville, in Crook County.{kbnd,orlive_17,bul11,nautilus} On November 9, 2011, the students' lawyer, Kelly Clark, brought a second suit in Multnomah County for 14 more former students, seeking $23 million, which brought the number suing to 31.{bul11,orlive_nov} A third suit, Doe 210 v. Mount Bachelor Educational Center (No. 12-cv-0008), was filed in Deschutes County on January 4, 2012, and the second and third were later moved to Crook County as well.{nautilus,bul15} In January 2014 The Bulletin counted 17 plaintiffs seeking $26 million in the first case, 15 seeking $22.85 million in the second and 13 seeking $19.5 million in the third.{bul14} The Bulletin later put the total at 51 former students seeking more than $48 million.{bul15} A 2009 Oregon law had raised the age limit for child sexual abuse claims from 24 to 40, and in January 2013 a judge let one case go forward despite a statute-of-limitations defense.{bul15} The suits were resolved privately under confidential terms and dismissed in September and November 2014.{bul15}
